title: Specialization and Hilbert irreducibility
subject: specialization
summary: Hilbert irreducibility preserves the generic Galois group outside a thin set. Geometry and restrictions on the parameters give more precise descriptions of the exceptions.
questionsAnswered: When does a specialization retain the generic Galois group?
Why can the exceptional set be infinite, and when can it be finite?
What changes when parameters are restricted to units?
Why can arithmetic and geometric Galois groups differ?

sections.title: Specialization of Galois groups
sections.body:
Fix a number field \(K\) and a monic, separable, irreducible polynomial \(F(T,x)\in K(T)[x]\). Its arithmetic group is \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(F/K(T))\), acting on the roots. Exclude the finitely many parameter values where a coefficient has a pole or the discriminant vanishes. At every other \(t\in K\), the specialized group \(G_t\) is conjugate to a subgroup of \(G\).

This inclusion comes from a decomposition group above the place \(T=t\) in the generic splitting field. The roots remain distinct, so the unramified residue action is the action on the specialized roots. The specialized group may be a proper subgroup of the generic group.

citations.note: Specialization of the root permutation action.

sections.title: Arithmetic and geometric groups
sections.body:
Let \(K\) have characteristic zero, let \(T\) be transcendental, and let \(L/K(T)\) be the splitting field of a separable polynomial. Inside a common algebraic closure, put \(C=L\cap\overline K\), the field of algebraic constants. Define

\[G_{\mathrm{arith}}=\operatorname{Gal}(L/K(T)),\qquad G_{\mathrm{geom}}=\operatorname{Gal}(L\overline K/\overline K(T)).\]

The constants exact sequence

The extension \(C/K\) is finite Galois, and restriction to constants gives

\[1\longrightarrow G_{\mathrm{geom}}\longrightarrow G_{\mathrm{arith}}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(C/K)\longrightarrow1.\]

Normality makes \(C\) stable under the arithmetic group, and automorphisms of \(C(T)/K(T)\) extend to \(L\). The kernel is \(\operatorname{Gal}(L/C(T))\). Since \(C\) is relatively algebraically closed in \(L\), the extension is regular over \(C\); extending constants to \(\overline K\) preserves this kernel. Thus the two groups agree exactly when \(C=K\), the regular case. The exact sequence need not split in general.

Example: \(X^3-T\) over \(\mathbb Q(T)\)

Choose \(\alpha^3=T\) and a primitive cube root \(\zeta\). The roots are \(\alpha,\zeta\alpha,\zeta^2\alpha\), so \(L=\mathbb Q(\zeta)(\alpha)\). Because \(\alpha\) is transcendental, this rational function field has algebraic constants exactly \(C=\mathbb Q(\zeta)=\mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})\). Eisenstein at \(T\) over \(C[T]\) gives

\[[L:\mathbb Q(T)]=[L:C(T)]\,[C(T):\mathbb Q(T)]=3\cdot2=6.\]

The automorphism \(r\) sends \(\alpha\mapsto\zeta\alpha\) and fixes \(\zeta\); the automorphism \(s\) fixes \(\alpha\) and sends \(\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{-1}\). They satisfy \(r^3=s^2=1\) and \(srs=r^{-1}\). Hence \(G_{\mathrm{arith}}\cong S_3\), while \(G_{\mathrm{geom}}=\langle r\rangle\cong C_3\). The quotient \(C_2\) acts on the quadratic constant field. The discriminant \(-27T^2=-3(3T)^2\) identifies the same quadratic constant field.

For comparison, \(X^3-X-T\) is irreducible over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}(T)\): apply Gauss’s lemma to its irreducibility as a polynomial linear in \(T\) with unit leading coefficient in \(\overline{\mathbb Q}[X,T]\). Its discriminant \(4-27T^2\) has two simple zeros, so is not a square in that rational function field. The cubic criterion gives \(G_{\mathrm{geom}}=S_3\); consequently \(G_{\mathrm{arith}}=S_3\) and \(C=\mathbb Q\). Thus this family is regular, whereas \(X^3-T\) is not.

citations.note: Restriction and extension of Galois automorphisms and change of base field; the constants exact sequence is derived here from these facts.
Regular Galois extensions preserve their group after extension of constants.
Cubic discriminant formula, cubic group criterion, and splitting field from one root and the discriminant; the two parameter examples are worked out explicitly here.

sections.title: Hilbert irreducibility
sections.body:
Theorem (Hilbert irreducibility)

For \(F\) as above, there is a thin set \(B\subset K\) such that every \(t\in K\setminus B\) is admissible, \(F(t,x)\) is irreducible, and \(G_t=G\) up to conjugacy. In particular, infinitely many parameters retain the generic group.

Here “thin” means contained in a finite union of finite sets and images of rational points under dominant, generically finite maps from geometrically integral curves to the parameter line of degree at least two. Such a set may be infinite. The fixed fields of proper subgroups of \(G\) define resolvent covers. If a specialization has a smaller group, an associated cover has a rational point above that parameter. Hilbert’s theorem gives parameters outside the union of these images.

citations.note: Original theorem; modern formulations use Hilbertian fields.
Full-group specialization outside a thin set over number fields.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example

Let \(F(T,x)=x^3-x-T\). The quotient \(\mathbb Q[T,x]/(F)\) is \(\mathbb Q[x]\), with \(T=x^3-x\). Hence \(F\) is irreducible in the polynomial ring and, by Gauss’s lemma, in \(\mathbb Q(T)[x]\). Its discriminant is

\[\Delta(T)=4-27T^2.\]

The two zeros of this rational function are simple, so it is not a square in \(\mathbb Q(T)\). A transitive cubic group with nonsquare discriminant is \(S_3\).

At \(t=1\), the reduction of \(x^3-x-1\) modulo \(2\) has no root, and its discriminant is \(-23\), giving \(S_3\) again. But every \(t=u^3-u\), with \(u\in\mathbb Q\), gives the rational root \(u\). The parameters \(t=u^3-u\) form precisely the reducible-fiber locus, an infinite subset of the full-group exceptional set. There are also irreducible exceptional fibers: at \(t=1/7\), the cubic remains irreducible but its discriminant is \(169/49\), giving \(A_3\).

citations.note: The transitive cubic group and discriminant criterion; calculations here are explicit.

sections.title: Finite exceptional sets
sections.body:
In some families, proper-subgroup resolvent covers give a finite exceptional set. If the corresponding curves have genus at least two, each has only finitely many rational points. The required genus bounds depend on the ramification and the subgroup structure.

Theorem (Hajir–Wong)

Fix a number field \(K\). For fixed \(n\ge5\), all but finitely many \(\alpha\in K\) give an irreducible generalized Laguerre polynomial \(L_n^{(\alpha)}\) whose group contains \(A_n\). For \(n\ge10\), the group is \(S_n\) outside a finite set.

Here the degree is fixed and the parameter varies. Fixing \(\alpha\) and letting \(n\) grow is a different problem. The argument does not generally determine the finite exceptional set effectively.

citations.note: The displayed thresholds are ≥5 and ≥10; the PDF page was checked visually.

sections.title: Power parameters
sections.body:
Hilbert irreducibility over all rational parameters does not by itself control a prescribed sequence such as \(2^n\). For \(X^2-t\), exactly the odd integers \(n\) make \(X^2-2^n\) irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\); their density is \(1/2\).

Theorem (Bary-Soroker–Garzoni–Matei, conditional on GRH)

Let \(f(\mathbf t,X)\in\mathbb Z[t_1,\ldots,t_r,X]\), with \(\deg_Xf\ge1\), satisfy the pullback condition: for every tuple \(m_i\ge1\),

\[f(t_1^{m_1},\ldots,t_r^{m_r},X)\text{ is irreducible in }\overline{\mathbb Q}[\mathbf t,X].\]

Fix \(a_i\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0,1,-1\}\). Assuming GRH, the proportion of exponent vectors \(\mathbf n\in([-N,N]\cap\mathbb Z)^r\) for which \(f(a_1^{n_1},\ldots,a_r^{n_r},X)\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\) tends to one as \(N\to\infty\).

The pullback condition excludes reducibility caused by a power substitution. For \(X^2-t\), substituting \(t=u^2\) already produces a factorization. The theorem concerns irreducibility. Preservation of the Galois group requires a resolvent-cover argument and its additional hypotheses.

For one parameter there is a stronger unconditional result. Under the same pullback condition with \(r=1\), Dèbes proves that \(f(a^n,X)\) is irreducible for all but finitely many integers \(n\), without GRH. His Theorem 1.2 shows that infinitely many reducible fibers force a reducible scaled power pullback; geometric (PB) excludes this. The proof uses Siegel’s theorem on integral points on curves. The exceptional exponents are finite in number, but the theorem does not give an effective list.

citations.note: Published theorem; GRH and absolute irreducibility of every power pullback are essential.

citations.locator: Theorem 1.2, p. 144; see also Bary-Soroker–Garzoni–Matei, §1 after Theorem 1.1

sections.title: Unit parameters
sections.body:
Preprint, 3 September 2026. Let \(\pi:X\to\mathbb P^1\) be a nonconstant morphism from a smooth projective irreducible curve over a number field \(K\), let \(S\) be a finite set of non-archimedean places of \(K\), and put \(U=\mathcal O_S^\times\). Let \(\operatorname{Red}(\pi)\) be the set of \(K\)-rational parameters with a reducible fiber, together with all \(K\)-rational branch values. Siksek–Stoll prove

\[U\cap\operatorname{Red}(\pi)=I\cup\bigcup_{j=1}^{k}\gamma_j U^{r_j},\qquad |I|<\infty,\quad \gamma_j\in U,\quad r_j\ge2.\]

The power cosets are effectively computable; the proof does not make the finite remainder \(I\) effective. This describes the exceptional unit parameters more precisely than thinness alone. For \(x^2-T\), the exceptional unit parameters are simply the squares \(U^2\): if a square in \(K\) is an \(S\)-unit, its square root is also an \(S\)-unit.

citations.note: Version 1; this is a preprint theorem, not a complete effective algorithm.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.body: Irreducibility of one fiber does not imply a uniform theorem in degree or determine all exceptional fibers. The arithmetic group over \(K(T)\) can exceed the geometric group over \(\overline K(T)\). A theorem at each finite iteration depth need not give one parameter valid at every depth. This requires control of an intersection of infinitely many Hilbert sets.

citations.note: Hilbertian fields and specialization framework.
A concrete warning against interchanging finite-level and infinite-level quantifiers.

sections.title: Dynatomic specializations
sections.body:
For \(f_T(x)=x^2+T\) and \(n\ge1\), put

\[\Phi_n(T,x)=\prod_{d\mid n}(f_T^{\circ d}(x)-x)^{\mu(n/d)}.\]

Over \(\mathbb Q(T)\), this polynomial is irreducible and its group is \(C_n\wr S_r\), where \(nr=\deg_x\Phi_n\). The action must commute with the permutation given by iteration, whose cycles all have length \(n\). This gives the upper bound \(C_n\wr S_r\); the generic group attains it. Let \(E_n\) be the rational parameters where the specialized group differs from the generic group. Krumm proves \(E_n\) finite for \(n=5,6,7,9\), whereas it is infinite for \(n\le4\). These finiteness proofs do not list all exceptional parameters.

sections.title: Period four
sections.body: For every quadratic \(f\in\mathbb Q[x]\), Krumm determines the Galois group and the degrees of the irreducible factors of its fourth dynatomic polynomial. Thus period four has an explicit classification, while the finiteness question above concerns larger periods. The proof uses subgroup computations and rational points on the corresponding specialization curves.

citations.locator: Abstract and classification of fourth dynatomic polynomials

sections.title: Local groups under specialization
sections.body:
Hilbert irreducibility controls the global group. Ramification imposes additional local conditions. Let \(E/K(T)\) be a finite Galois extension, regular over a number field \(K\), and let \(t_i\in K\) be a finite branch point. Write \(I_i\triangleleft D_i\) for its inertia and decomposition groups and \(\pi_i:D_i\to D_i/I_i\) for the quotient map. The residue extension at \(t_i\) has group \(D_i/I_i\).

Let \(t_0\in K\) be a nonbranch specialization point. Outside a finite set of primes, suppose \(t_0,t_i\) are integral at \(\mathfrak p\), \(a=v_{\mathfrak p}(t_0-t_i)>0\), and \(\gcd(a,|I_i|)=1\). If \(D_{i,\mathfrak p}\) denotes the decomposition group in the branch-point residue extension, then the decomposition group of the specialization at \(\mathfrak p\) is conjugate to \(\pi_i^{-1}(D_{i,\mathfrak p})\). This gives a method for prescribing local behavior while seeking specializations with the full global group.

citations.locator: Theorem 1.1; Theorem 4.1 for the more general statement

sections.title: Computing the geometric group
sections.body: Over \(\mathbb Q(t)\), Fieker–Sutherland compute the field of algebraic constants and the geometric group. These determine both the kernel and quotient of the constants exact sequence above; the arithmetic group alone does not determine them.

sections.title: Curves for exceptional specializations
sections.body:
Let \(P(t,x)\in\mathbb Q[t,x]\) be separable over \(\mathbb Q(t)\), with nontrivial generic group \(G\). For representatives \(M_i\) of the conjugacy classes of maximal subgroups, choose monic polynomials \(F_i(t,y)\in\mathbb Q[t,y]\) defining the fixed fields \(L^{M_i}\). Exclude values where the leading coefficient or discriminant of \(P\), or a discriminant of \(F_i\), vanishes.

Krumm–Sutherland prove that the specialized group is smaller than \(G\) exactly when some \(F_i(c,y)\) has a rational root. Thus exceptional parameters come from rational points on finitely many explicit curves. Constructing these curves does not, in general, compute all their rational points.

For \(c\in\mathbb Q\), their examples prove that \(x^6+c^6-1\) is reducible exactly when \(c=0,1,-1\).

questions.title: Can the finite exceptional parameters be determined effectively?
questions.scope: A specified one-parameter family over a fixed number field
questions.body: A finiteness theorem need not determine the exceptional parameters effectively. Hajir–Wong discuss this difficulty for their curves; the 2026 unit-specialization theorem also leaves a finite set ineffective. For a given family, the problem reduces to determining rational or integral points on the associated curves.

questions.title: Are the exceptional dynatomic specializations finite for every period n>4?
questions.body: Krumm proposes finiteness for every \(n>4\) and proves it for \(5,6,7,9\). Determining each exceptional set explicitly is a further problem.

title: Inverse Galois theory and generic polynomials
subject: specialization
summary: The inverse Galois problem asks which finite groups occur over a given field. Regular realizations and generic polynomials impose further conditions on families of extensions.
questionsAnswered: What does it mean to realize a finite group by a polynomial?
How do regular realizations and generic polynomials differ?

sections.title: Realizations and parametrizations
sections.body:
The inverse Galois problem over \(K\) asks whether a given finite group \(G\) is \(\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)\) for some finite Galois extension. One may also ask for an explicit polynomial whose splitting field is \(L\). A regular realization over \(K(T)\) requires \(L\cap\overline K=K\). Thus the constant field remains unchanged.

A polynomial \(P(\mathbf T,x)\) is parametric for \(G\) over \(K\) if its generic splitting group is \(G\) and every \(G\)-extension of \(K\) is obtained by specialization. It is generic if this remains true over every extension field of \(K\). A family with group \(G\) at infinitely many parameters need not parametrize all \(G\)-extensions.

citations.note: Parametric versus generic; existence versus construction.

sections.title: Regular realizations
sections.body:
Regular realization and specialization

A regular finite Galois extension of \(K(T)\) with nontrivial group \(G\), for \(K\) a number field, gives infinitely many linearly disjoint \(G\)-extensions of \(K\) by Hilbert irreducibility.

Regular realizations can be constructed using invariant fields, branched covers and rigidity, embedding problems, or arithmetic families such as torsion on elliptic curves. The cover must have the required geometric group, descend to the chosen base field, and be regular there. Hilbert irreducibility then gives arithmetic specializations. A complex cover with group \(G\) does not by itself give a \(G\)-extension of \(\mathbb Q\).

citations.note: Linear disjointness from a regular family.
Rigidity, embedding problems, and geometric constructions.

sections.title: Examples
sections.body:
Examples

If \(\operatorname{char}K\ne2\), the polynomial \(x^2-T\) is generic for \(C_2\): every quadratic extension of every field \(E\supseteq K\) has the form \(E(\sqrt a)\) for a nonsquare \(a\in E\). The exceptional specializations \(T=a\in E^2\) split. A generic polynomial may therefore have specializations with a smaller group.

For a cyclic cubic extension of \(\mathbb Q\), take

\[f=x^3+x^2-2x-1.\]

The rational-root candidates \(\pm1\) are not roots, so \(f\) is irreducible. Its discriminant is \(49\), hence the transitive group lies in \(A_3=C_3\) and is exactly \(C_3\). A root is \(\zeta_7+\zeta_7^{-1}\), which generates the real cubic subfield of \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_7)\).

citations.note: Cubic discriminant test; the explicit calculations are included here.
Cyclotomic extensions and quadratic extensions.

sections.title: Existence results
sections.body:
Every finite solvable group occurs over \(\mathbb Q\) by Shafarevich’s theorem. Symmetric and alternating groups also occur over \(\mathbb Q\), as Hilbert proved. The general assertion for every finite group remains open in the cited sources. The regular inverse Galois problem is stronger.

An explicit realization also specifies a faithful permutation action. A transitive action of degree \(n\) corresponds to a degree-\(n\) irreducible polynomial whose splitting group acts in that way. The regular action has degree \(|G|\), often much larger than the smallest degree of a faithful transitive action. Databases of number fields therefore organize groups by degree and transitive action, not only abstract isomorphism type.

citations.note: Hilbert and Shafarevich existence theorems.
Explicit realizations of transitive permutation groups.
The ordinary and regular inverse problems.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.body:
A finite list of examples realizes only the listed groups and actions. Even a complete computation up to a degree bound leaves the general inverse problem unresolved. Failure to find a polynomial does not establish nonexistence. A generic polynomial requires a proof that every extension in the stated class occurs by specialization.

For a polynomial family, symmetry often bounds the Galois group from above. Irreducibility, local cycle types, and resolvents can then determine the group. A separate argument is needed to determine which extensions occur among its specializations.

questions.title: Does every finite group occur as a Galois group over Q?
questions.scope: Finite Galois extensions of Q; no fixed degree bound
questions.body: This is the classical inverse Galois problem. The cited monographs describe known realizations. For a specified group, one can also ask for a realization in a prescribed transitive action.

citations.note: Inverse Galois problem and known realizations.

questions.title: Does every finite group admit a regular realization over Q(T)?
questions.scope: Regular finite Galois extensions of Q(T)
questions.body: This is Serre’s Conjecture 4.1.1. A positive answer would imply the ordinary inverse Galois problem by specialization. The conjecture concerns finite groups, not arbitrary profinite groups.

title: Composition, iteration, and arboreal groups
subject: dynamics
summary: Polynomial composition gives extension towers and Galois actions on rooted trees. Irreducibility of all iterates is weaker than surjectivity of the arboreal representation.
questionsAnswered: Why do iterated Galois groups lie in wreath products?
Which arithmetic conditions control the group at every level?

sections.title: Factorization and composition
sections.body:
Multiplicative factorization \(f=gh\) differs from composition \(f=g\circ h\). In composition theory, the factors are nonconstant maps and the units are linear changes of variable. For example, \(x^4=(x^2)\circ(x^2)\), whereas every nonconstant polynomial over \(\mathbb C\) factors multiplicatively into linear factors. Ritt’s “prime” polynomials are indecomposable under composition.

For \(f\in\mathbb C[x]\), composition is connected to intermediate fields of \(\mathbb C(x)/\mathbb C(f(x))\) and to blocks in the monodromy action of \(f(x)-T\). This is a function-field group, not the splitting group of the particular polynomial \(f(x)\) over \(\mathbb Q\).

citations.note: Functional decomposition; consult the recorded erratum.
Primitive monodromy of complex polynomial maps.

sections.title: Capelli’s lemma
sections.body:
Theorem (Capelli’s composition lemma)

Let \(F\in K[x]\) be irreducible of degree \(m\), let \(g\in K[x]\) have degree \(d\ge1\), and let \(\alpha\) be a root of \(F\). Then \(F(g(x))\) is irreducible over \(K\) if and only if \(g(x)-\alpha\) is irreducible over \(K(\alpha)\).

For a root \(\beta\) of \(g(x)-\alpha\), we have \(\alpha=g(\beta)\), so \(K(\alpha)\subseteq K(\beta)\). The tower law gives \([K(\beta):K]=m[K(\beta):K(\alpha)]\). This equals \(md=\deg(F\circ g)\) exactly when \(g(x)-\alpha\) is a scalar multiple of a minimal polynomial of degree \(d\). This proves both implications.

The criterion reduces the problem to factorization over a root field. For quadratic iterates, this requires deciding whether certain elements are squares in that field.

citations.note: Composition and reducibility; the field-degree proof is given in full here.
Composition as the starting point for iterated Galois theory.

sections.title: Rooted trees and wreath products
sections.body:
Let \(f\in K[x]\) have degree \(d\ge2\), and suppose each iterate \(f^{\circ n}\) is separable. Put a separate copy of its roots at level \(n\), with an edge from \(\beta\) to \(f(\beta)\). The resulting regular rooted \(d\)-ary tree is preserved by Galois, because every automorphism commutes with evaluation of \(f\).

\[G_n\ \le\ \operatorname{Aut}(T_{d,n})\cong [S_d]^n,\qquad |\operatorname{Aut}(T_{d,n})|=(d!)^{1+d+\cdots+d^{n-1}}.\]

The right side is an iterated wreath product, generally much smaller than \(S_{d^n}\). Irreducibility of every iterate, called stability, is equivalent to transitivity at every level. Surjectivity onto the tree automorphism group is stronger.

citations.note: The preimage tree, arboreal representation, and natural maximal group.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example

For \(f=x^2+1\), the first iterate is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\), and

\[f^{\circ2}=x^4+2x^2+2\]

is Eisenstein at \(2\). Its four roots fall into two pairs according to whether \(f(\beta)=i\) or \(-i\). Thus its group is contained in \(C_2\wr C_2\), of order eight.

The quadratic critical-orbit criterion uses \(c_1=-a\) and \(c_n=f_a^{\circ n}(0)\) for \(n\ge2\), where \(f_a=x^2+a\) and \(a\in\mathbb Q\setminus\{0,-1\}\). It says that the level-\(n\) group is full precisely when \(c_1,\ldots,c_n\) are independent in \(\mathbb Q^\times/\mathbb Q^{\times2}\). Here \((c_1,c_2)=(-1,2)\); none of \(-1,2,-2\) is a rational square. Consequently \(G_2=C_2\wr C_2\), the dihedral group of order eight. This calculation determines only the first two levels.

citations.note: Square-class criterion for quadratic iterates; restated in Stoll2026 Proposition1.7.

sections.title: Postcritically finite polynomials
sections.body:
A polynomial is postcritically finite (PCF) when every critical point has finite forward orbit. For \(f=x^2-2\), the finite critical orbit is \(0\mapsto-2\mapsto2\mapsto2\). Every iterate is nevertheless irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\).

Proof

The identity \(f(z+z^{-1})=z^2+z^{-2}\) gives

\[f^{\circ n}(z+z^{-1})=z^{2^n}+z^{-2^n}.\]

For a primitive \(2^{n+2}\)-th root of unity \(\zeta\), the element \(\zeta+\zeta^{-1}\) is therefore a root of \(f^{\circ n}\). It has degree \(\varphi(2^{n+2})/2=2^n\), the degree of the iterate. All its conjugates lie in the same real cyclotomic field, so

\[K_n=\mathbb Q(\zeta+\zeta^{-1}),\qquad G_n\cong C_{2^n}.\]

Thus the action is transitive at every level, whereas \(|G_n|=2^n\) is much smaller than \(|\operatorname{Aut}(T_{2,n})|=2^{2^n-1}\) for \(n\ge2\).

Benedetto–Ghioca–Juul–Tucker describe the ambient groups imposed by PCF relations and give criteria for attaining them: the 2025 paper treats periodic critical points; its 2026 companion treats strictly preperiodic ones. These groups depend on critical-orbit relations, the base field, and the target point. The latter paper treats the classical Chebyshev case above separately from its general constructions.

citations.note: Periodic PCF case; maximality is inside the constrained group M, not the full binary-tree group.
§1.4 explicitly separates x²−2 and records the Chebyshev identity; the cyclotomic calculation at target zero is supplied here.

sections.title: Generic and arithmetic groups
sections.body:
For the generic monic degree-\(d\) polynomial \(F=x^d+s_{d-1}x^{d-1}+\cdots+s_0\) over a characteristic-zero field \(k\), with algebraically independent coefficients \(s_0,\ldots,s_{d-1}\), Odoni proves \(\operatorname{Gal}(F^{\circ n}/k(\mathbf s))=[S_d]^n\) for every fixed \(n\). Juul extends this to positive characteristic, excluding \((d,\operatorname{char}k)=(2,2)\) for polynomials. The induction uses disjoint ramification in the new branches to obtain independent permutations.

Over number fields, Benedetto–Juul prove all-level existence in every even degree and in odd degree when \([K:\mathbb Q]\) is odd. Specter’s 2018 preprint states all degrees over every number field. In contrast, Dittmann–Kadets construct characteristic-zero Hilbertian fields admitting no finite-index arboreal image. Thus the existence theorem depends on the base field.

citations.note: Characteristic-zero generic theorem.
Positive-characteristic exception and generic full wreath products.
Published number-field cases.
All-degree number-field statement, labeled as a preprint.
General Hilbertian-field counterexample.

sections.title: Finite-level detection
sections.body:
Preprint submitted 10 November 2026. Stoll gives revised proofs and rational-parameter extensions of maximality criteria for \(x^2+a\). Proposition 1.7 restates the square-class test. Theorem 6.1 gives explicit regions and congruence classes where maximality at level two implies maximality at every level. Its hypotheses do not include every rational \(a\).

The paper also formulates a uniform finite-level detection conjecture and reports supporting computations. These finite calculations do not prove the conjecture for all parameters. Relations among critical-orbit square classes can cause the first failure of maximality at a later level.

Example

For \(a=2/3\), the first four adjusted critical values are

\[(c_1,c_2,c_3,c_4)=\left(-\frac23,\frac{10}{9},\frac{154}{81},\frac{28090}{6561}\right).\]

The first three square classes are independent: the sign detects \(c_1\), the prime \(5\) detects \(c_2\), and the prime \(7\) detects \(c_3\). But \(c_2c_4=(530/243)^2\). Hence the level-three group is full and the level-four group is not. A universal detection level, if one exists, must therefore be at least four.

citations.note: arXiv:2611.14014v1, 10 November 2026. The a=2/3 relation is checked directly; it is an exact obstruction, not evidence from a finite numerical search.

sections.title: Eventual stability
sections.body: Eventual stability means that the number of irreducible factors of \(f^{\circ n}\) stays bounded as \(n\) grows; individual iterates may be reducible. For \(f=x^2+1/c\), \(c\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0,-1\}\), DeMark and coauthors prove the predicted bound of four factors for \(|c|\le10^9\). They also verify their second-iterate stability criterion for \(|c|\le10^{1000}\). These are all-iterate theorems within bounded parameter ranges.

sections.title: Local criteria for eventual stability
sections.body:
For \(f\in K[x]\), eventual stability means that the numbers of irreducible factors of \(f^{\circ n}\), counted with multiplicity, are bounded. Hamblen–Jones–Madhu prove this for \(f=x^d+c\in\mathbb Q[x]\), \(d\ge2\), whenever \(c\ne0\) is not the reciprocal of an integer. Their proof controls how a factor can split under further composition by using valuations of critical-orbit values.

Jones–Levy give a different local criterion. Over a discretely valued field with finite residue field of characteristic \(p\), a rational map with good reduction to \(M(x^{p^j})\), where \(j\ge1\) and \(M\) is an invertible fractional linear map over the residue field, is eventually stable at every nonperiodic target. In particular, \(x^2+1/a\) is eventually stable over \(\mathbb Q\) for odd \(a\ne-1\).

sections.title: A nonperiodic target need not give eventual stability
sections.body:
The original Jones–Levy conjecture allowed any target that was not periodic. This is stronger than requiring an infinite forward orbit. For \(\phi(x)=x^6\) and target \(-1\), the orbit is \(-1\mapsto1\mapsto1\), but

\[\phi^{\circ n}(x)+1=x^{6^n}+1=\prod_{j=0}^{n}\Phi_{2^{n+1}3^j}(x).\]

Here \(\Phi_m\) is the \(m\)-th cyclotomic polynomial. Indeed, the divisors of \(2\cdot6^n\) that do not divide \(6^n\) are exactly \(2^{n+1}3^j\), \(0\le j\le n\). Cyclotomic irreducibility gives exactly \(n+1\) factors over \(\mathbb Q\), so eventual stability fails. This direct calculation does not contradict the reciprocal-quadratic questions above.

Tucker–Zhu’s October 2026 preprint reports a counterexample and a classification for power maps. Theorem 1.2 gives the displayed example, whose factorization is verified by the argument above.

questions.title: Can one fixed iterate detect the full arboreal group?
questions.scope: f_a=x²+a with a∈Q∖{−1,0}; target point 0; Stoll, November 2026.
questions.body:
Let \(T_n\) be the binary tree of preimages of \(0\) through level \(n\), and let \(T_\infty\) be the full tree. Does some integer \(N\), independent of \(a\), satisfy

\[\operatorname{Gal}(f_a^{\circ N}/\mathbb Q)=\operatorname{Aut}(T_N)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad G_\infty(f_a,0)=\operatorname{Aut}(T_\infty)?\]

Hindes asks the equivalent question at the end of §3, including the sharper proposal \(N=4\). Stoll restates it as Conjecture 8.1. The values \(a=2/3\) and \(a=-6/7\) have maximal groups at level 3 but not level 4, so \(N<4\) cannot work. Proposition 8.2 verifies the implication from level 4 to level 20 for every rational parameter of height at most \(10^6\), where \(H(r/s)=\max(|r|,s)\) in lowest terms with \(s>0\). This finite computation does not prove the all-level assertion.

citations.note: Asks whether the first failure of maximality can occur at arbitrarily large levels, and whether all first failures occur before level 5.

citations.locator: Conjecture 8.1, Proposition 8.2, and Remark 8.5; arXiv:2611.14014v1 (10 November 2026)

questions.title: Does every Hilbertian field admit a surjective arboreal representation?
questions.scope: General Hilbertian fields of characteristic zero
questions.body: No. Dittmann–Kadets give counterexample fields. These counterexamples are compatible with the positive existence results over number fields and with generic maximality at each fixed finite level.

questions.title: Does every quadratic polynomial with infinite critical orbit have finite-index arboreal image?
questions.scope: f=x²+c over a number field K; the forward orbit of 0 is infinite; target point 0
questions.body: Let \(T_\infty\) be the full binary tree of preimages of \(0\). The polynomial case of Jones’s finite-index conjecture predicts \([\operatorname{Aut}(T_\infty):G_\infty(f,0)]<\infty\). This allows a proper subgroup at early levels. The hypothesis excludes the postcritically finite examples, and it also ensures that every preimage level is separable. The general statement is open in the cited survey.

title: Irreducibility over finite fields
subject: finite-fields
summary: Frobenius powers give an exact irreducibility criterion and a formula for the number of irreducible polynomials. Primitive polynomials satisfy an additional multiplicative-order condition.
questionsAnswered: How can irreducibility be certified without a full factorization?
How many monic irreducibles of a given degree exist?
Why is the Galois group cyclic, and what does primitive mean?

sections.title: The Frobenius identity
sections.body:
Let \(q\) be a prime power. In \(\mathbb F_q[x]\),

\[x^{q^m}-x=\prod_{\substack{P\text{ monic irreducible}\\\deg P\mid m}}P(x).\]

Every element of \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) is a root, the derivative is \(-1\), and an element of degree \(d\) over \(\mathbb F_q\) belongs to \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\) exactly when \(d\mid m\). Thus each indicated factor occurs once.

If \(f\) is irreducible of degree \(n\), adjoining one root gives \(\mathbb F_{q^n}\), which already contains every conjugate. Its Galois group is \(C_n\), generated by \(z\mapsto z^q\). Noncyclic monodromy groups over finite fields arise over function fields such as \(\mathbb F_q(T)\), not this constant-field extension.

citations.note: Finite-field structure and irreducible polynomials.
A contrasting function-field monodromy setting.

sections.title: The irreducibility criterion
sections.body:
Theorem (Frobenius-power criterion)

A monic polynomial \(f\in\mathbb F_q[x]\) of degree \(n\ge1\) is irreducible if and only if

\[x^{q^n}\equiv x\pmod f,\qquad \gcd\bigl(f,x^{q^{n/\ell}}-x\bigr)=1\quad\text{for every prime }\ell\mid n.\]

The first condition makes \(f\) squarefree and forces every factor degree to divide \(n\). If a proper divisor \(d\mid n\) occurred as a factor degree, some prime \(\ell\mid n/d\) would give \(d\mid n/\ell\), contradicting the corresponding gcd. The reverse implication follows from the same Frobenius identity. The criterion uses modular exponentiation and Euclidean gcds, without expanding the powers as polynomials.

citations.note: Irreducibility testing in finite-field algorithms.

citations.locator: Irreducibility testing over finite fields, Theorem 1
citations.note: Official documentation states the criterion and its exact algorithmic use.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example

Take \(f=x^4+x+1\in\mathbb F_2[x]\). Repeated squaring modulo \(f\) gives

\[x^4\equiv x+1,\qquad x^8\equiv x^2+1,\qquad x^{16}\equiv x.\]

The only prime divisor of \(n=4\) is \(2\), and \(x^4-x\equiv1\pmod f\). Thus the required gcd is one, and \(f\) is irreducible. Its splitting field has 16 elements, and the Galois group over \(\mathbb F_2\) has order four.

The congruence \(x^{16}\equiv x\pmod f\) alone does not suffice: the reducible quartic \(x^4+x=x(x+1)(x^2+x+1)\) also divides \(x^{16}-x\). The gcd conditions eliminate smaller-degree factors.

citations.note: Application of the exact criterion; the displayed remainders are direct calculations.

sections.title: Counting irreducible polynomials
sections.body:
If \(N_q(n)\) counts monic irreducibles of degree \(n\), taking degrees in the Frobenius identity and applying Möbius inversion gives

\[N_q(n)=\frac1n\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)q^{n/d}.\]

For example, \(N_2(4)=(16-4)/4=3\). For fixed \(q\) and large \(n\), the proportion of monic degree-\(n\) polynomials that are irreducible is asymptotic to \(1/n\). Random sampling followed by exact testing gives a construction algorithm. Shoup and others also study deterministic constructions and faster algorithms.

citations.note: Counting formula from Möbius inversion.
Algorithms for constructing irreducible polynomials.
Fast constructions.

sections.title: Primitive polynomials and prescribed coefficients
sections.body:
An irreducible polynomial of degree \(n\) is primitive if a root generates \(\mathbb F_{q^n}^{\times}\), a group of order \(q^n-1\). Primitivity concerns the multiplicative order of a root; the Galois group remains cyclic, with order equal to the degree of the polynomial. For the quartic above, the root \(\alpha\) has order 15: \(\alpha^3\ne1\) and \(\alpha^5=\alpha^2+\alpha\ne1\), excluding the proper maximal divisors 5 and 3 of 15.

Prescribed coefficients, sparse support, and primitivity impose different restrictions on the counting problem. The Hansen–Mullen primitivity problem is stronger than its irreducibility problem. Wan’s theorem and the finite checks of Ham–Mullen concern irreducibility; Tuxanidy–Wang give a later proof. Results on several prescribed coefficients have restrictions on the parameters. In particular, a zero constant coefficient precludes irreducibility in degree greater than one.

citations.note: Primitive polynomials and prescribed coefficients.
Hansen–Mullen irreducibility theorem outside finitely many cases.
Completion of the remaining finite cases.
A later proof of the irreducibility theorem.
Several prescribed coefficients; the range is approximately a square root of the degree, not the full degree.

sections.title: Discriminants and factor parity
sections.body: For a squarefree polynomial of degree \(n\) with \(r\) irreducible factors over a finite field of odd order, Frobenius has sign \((-1)^{n-r}\). Its discriminant is a square exactly when \(n-r\) is even. This is the Stickelberger discriminant-parity theorem. Swan develops its characteristic-two lifting form and applies it to trinomials. The required parity may still allow several factors, so it does not prove irreducibility.

citations.note: The basic theorem is credited by Swan to Stickelberger, with Dalen’s prior proof noted.

questions.scope: A specified finite field, degree, and support

A prescribed support or coefficient pattern may force factors, and existence must then be studied for that pattern. Exact certificates can establish individual cases; a general result requires a uniform argument.

title: Absolute irreducibility and Newton polytopes
subject: multivariate
summary: An indecomposable Newton polytope can prove absolute irreducibility. When the polytope decomposes, factorization depends on the coefficients.
questionsAnswered: How does absolute irreducibility differ from irreducibility over the ground field?
When does the Newton polytope certify absolute irreducibility?
Why does a decomposable polytope leave irreducibility undecided?

sections.title: Absolute irreducibility
sections.body:
A nonconstant \(f\in K[x_1,\ldots,x_r]\) is absolutely irreducible if it remains irreducible over \(\overline K\). For a univariate polynomial this forces degree one. In several variables, this means that the coordinate ring of the hypersurface defined by \(f\) remains a domain after extension to \(\overline K\). Equivalently, the hypersurface is geometrically integral.

For example, \(x^2+y^2\) is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\) but factors over \(\mathbb Q(i)\) as \((x+iy)(x-iy)\). Irreducibility over the ground field therefore does not imply absolute irreducibility. Irreducibility and smoothness of the hypersurface are also distinct properties.

citations.note: Absolute irreducibility of multivariate polynomials.
Rational and absolute factorization in several variables.

sections.title: Newton polytopes and products
sections.body:
For \(f=\sum_{\mathbf a}c_{\mathbf a}x^{\mathbf a}\), its Newton polytope is

\[\operatorname{Newt}(f)=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{r}:c_{\mathbf a}\ne0\}.\]

For a product, \(\operatorname{Newt}(gh)=\operatorname{Newt}(g)+\operatorname{Newt}(h)\), where the right side is the Minkowski sum. For a linear weight with unique maxima on the two factor polytopes, the product of the highest-weight terms is nonzero and is the unique highest-weight term of the product. Varying the weight determines the polytope and proves the identity.

A lattice polytope is integrally indecomposable if every expression as a sum of two lattice polytopes has a point as one summand. A point polytope corresponds to a monomial, not necessarily to a constant.

citations.note: Product formula, with its origin attributed to Ostrowski, and the monomial caveat.

sections.title: The indecomposability criterion
sections.body:
Theorem (Newton-polytope criterion)

Let \(f\in K[x_1,\ldots,x_r]\) be nonconstant and divisible by no variable \(x_i\). If \(\operatorname{Newt}(f)\) is integrally indecomposable, then \(f\) is absolutely irreducible.

Any factorization over \(\overline K\) decomposes the same lattice polytope. One factor must therefore have point support and be a monomial. Since no variable divides \(f\), that factor is a nonzero constant. This excludes every nontrivial factorization.

The criterion depends only on the support. It remains valid after changing the nonzero coefficients, over any field, provided the support is unchanged.

citations.note: Integral indecomposability criterion; the elementary proof is included.
Explicit statement excluding divisibility by any variable.

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example

Consider \(f=1+x^2y+xy^3\) over any field. Its Newton polygon has vertices \((0,0),(2,1),(1,3)\). The oriented edge vectors are \((2,1),(-1,2),(-1,-3)\), all primitive integer vectors.

A nontrivial Minkowski summand of a triangle must itself be a triangle with parallel corresponding edges; a segment summand would introduce another edge direction. The two triangular summands would therefore divide each edge into two positive integral lengths. A primitive edge has lattice length one, so this is impossible. The polygon is integrally indecomposable. The nonzero constant term excludes nonconstant monomial factors. The criterion therefore proves absolute irreducibility in every characteristic.

citations.note: Triangle indecomposability criteria; this particular support is checked explicitly here.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.body:
Monomial factors. The polynomial \(x(1+x+y)\) has a translated indecomposable triangle as its Newton polygon, but has a nonconstant monomial factor. The hypothesis excluding variable divisors is essential.

The converse is false. Over a field of characteristic different from two, \(x^2+y^2+1\) is absolutely irreducible, although its polygon is twice the standard simplex and hence decomposable. Its projective homogenization \(X^2+Y^2+Z^2\) is nonsingular; a reducible projective conic over an algebraically closed field is a pair of lines, possibly repeated, and is singular. In characteristic two this example becomes \((x+y+1)^2\), so the characteristic restriction is necessary.

citations.note: A decomposable polytope makes the shape test inconclusive; the examples are direct checks.

sections.title: Coefficient criteria and differential methods
sections.body:
If the polytope decomposes, the coefficients determine whether a factorization exists. Effective Noether forms describe the reducibility locus. Fix a total-degree bound \(d\ge1\). There are finitely many integer polynomials in the coefficient variables such that all of them vanish exactly when the specialized polynomial is reducible over the algebraic closure or its total degree drops below \(d\). Thus, for a polynomial of exact degree \(d\), absolute irreducibility is certified by at least one nonzero Noether form. In positive characteristic, reduce the integer coefficients of the forms modulo that characteristic. Differential methods instead recover factor information through linear systems. For a squarefree bivariate \(f=\prod_i f_i\) in characteristic zero, the identity

\[\frac{df}{f}=\sum_i\frac{df_i}{f_i}\]

suggests looking for closed rational one-forms with denominator \(f\). Writing such a form as \((g/f)\,dx+(h/f)\,dy\) gives the polynomial linear equation

\[f\,(g_y-h_x)=g f_y-h f_x.\]

An algorithm based on this equation requires degree bounds and hypotheses on the characteristic. Gao’s paper develops the method in characteristic zero or sufficiently large characteristic; small characteristic requires separate arguments.

The polytope criterion can be applied before methods that use the coefficients. A reducible specialization \(f(x,t)\) does not establish that \(f(x,y)\) itself is reducible.

citations.note: Vanishing describes absolute reducibility together with degree drop; the fixed-degree qualification is essential.
Differential-equation factorization with characteristic restrictions.

questions.body: A decomposition of the polytope gives possible supports of factors, but does not determine whether those factors exist. For a specified family, one can study the reducibility locus in coefficient space or combine the support conditions with differential or lifting methods. The question concerns criteria adapted to that family, rather than a general factorization algorithm.
